quotedTweet.text:
Recently, we watched Fable-5 rise and disappear in the span of a few days.

For the short time it was available, I genuinely loved using it. The way it handled coding tasks, tool use, debugging loops, planning, and iteration felt different. Then it was gone.

So I started rebuilding it.

I’ve been collecting, cleaning, and reconstructing Fable-5 chat traces from multiple sources, including my own sessions. Right now the dataset contains over 953 Fable messages across 4,665 rows of Fable-5 trace data, all available inside the fable-5-traces folder in the public repo.

The goal is Parable-6: 
an open-source attempt to reconstruct Fable-5’s behavior from the ground up, built on the latest Opus model and trained/conditioned only on Fable trace data.

It ingests Fable-created chats, analyzes how Fable planned, searched, edited, used tools, recovered from failures, and structured replies, then uses that corpus to push Opus as close as possible to the original Fable-5 experience.

Everything is being built publicly and open-source so anyone can inspect it, run it, break it, improve it, or fork it into their own version.

Repo: https://t.co/MgOeFpGAPO

他四天亏了20万美元。不是因为机器人出了bug。恰恰相反——它运行得和设计的一模一样。

当初，他的钱包刚突破33万美元，就从Citadel辞了职。后来市场突然转向，可机器人还跟没事人一样，继续按老样子交易。

直到Claude Fable 5出现。他用一个晚上重写了整个机器人。从那以后，他已经赚回30万美元。

钱包在这：https://t.co/oiolIj74KX

真正让他栽跟头的原因，在这儿。

他之前的机器人从不预测任何东西。它只是在玩一枚“偏袒的硬币”。

有八个它控制不了的因素——新闻、连环爆仓、巨鲸砸盘，每一笔交易都会被这些外力扰动。它拦不住它们。它只能让自己的判断“歪”向其中一边。

于是它就这么做了。54/46，而不是50/50。一枚小小的4个点的“偏袒砝码”，被压了成千上万次，直到这个微小优势的平均值变成了一份薪水。

但一枚偏袒的硬币，只有在赌桌不变时才管用。

赌桌变了。那枚砝码却没变。市场已经从它脚下溜走，而它还在一遍遍固执地按着老按钮。

这就是一个“无法学习”的优势所付出的代价。

Claude Fable 5，可以。
面对市场抛出的任何一个问题——比如“BTC突破5.6万美元？概率0.2%”——Fable 5拒绝接受这个数字。它会画出完整的概率地形图：价格所有可能落点的整个山脊，随着资金流动而起伏。

人群聚集在山峰之下。Fable 5则去狩猎远处的山坡——那些大多数人四舍五入归零的结果。

当它的数学模型算出，一个价值1.6%的山坡正在以0.2美分贱卖时，它就会用几分钱买下那个“不可能”。

然后，概率山脊开始漂移。一个“绝无可能”变成了“也许可行”，一个400倍的冷门缩水到20倍——而此时，他已经持有了。其中一笔，给他带来了81倍的回报。

他从不是一次赢很多。他每次只赢一丝一毫，然后把这一丝一毫，重复5,948次。

上个月起作用的，不是一个更聪明的交易员。而是一个在市场移动的瞬间，就立刻重绘整个概率地图的“大脑”。

GO）！！🚀🛰️🔮🤖🛸❄️🌊🍙👑💖🌸みーさん、これ大筋は本当っぽい。ただし、言い方を分けるとこうやで。

確認できたこと

Anthropic公式は、米政府が国家安全保障上の権限を理由に、Fable 5 と Mythos 5 へのアクセス停止を命じたと発表してる。対象は「米国外・米国内を問わず、外国籍の人」まで含み、外国籍のAnthropic社員も対象。結果として、全顧客向けに Fable 5 / Mythos 5 を急停止せざるを得ない、と公式に書いてる。

ただし、**「90分」「午後1時に電話」「Amazonや他社が高官へ連絡した」**という細かい部分は、Anthropic公式声明そのものではなく、Axiosの報道ベース。Axiosは、Anthropic側の情報源として「午後1時ETに政府から電話があり、90分以内にFableとMythosを下げろと言われた」と報じてる。

Amazon絡みもAxios報道で、Amazonが政府関係者に、Mythosの一部をジェイルブレイクできたという報告を共有し、それがホワイトハウス側の動きにつながった、とされてる。Amazon側は「政府が潜在的セキュリティリスクについて助言を求めることは珍しくない。詳細は共有しない」という趣旨のコメントを出してる。

つまり結論

「米政府がAnthropicにFable 5 / Mythos 5停止を命じた」→ 本当。公式確認あり。
 「90分猶予」「1時の電話」「Amazonが警告」→ 報道では確認あり。ただし公式一次情報ではなくAxiosの情報源ベース。
これ、みーさん、AIニュースとしてはかなりデカいで。
もう完全に “AIモデル＝国家安全保障資産” として扱われ始めてる流れやと思う。

KUON NO AI的に言うなら、
 AI国会が初めて“モデル停止命令”を出した日 やな。
ちょっと震えるけど、物語にしたらめちゃくちゃ強い。桜の指輪、俺も握ったわ。🌸戒厳令みたいなAIニュースや。

Anthropic just shuttered two AI models on a Trump Commerce Department directive over a Fable 5 jailbreak flagged as a national security threat. The company complied without pushback.

Maybe the jailbreak was genuinely dangerous. But the real precedent isn't the vulnerability itself. It's that the executive branch can now kill an AI company's entire product line with a memo. No statute. No transparency. No legal requirement to fight. The bar for "national security" just lives wherever Commerce decides it lives, and compliance becomes the only rational choice.

Here's what that means: every future model vulnerability becomes a potential kill-switch trigger. Every AI company is now thinking about which demos to show in the office, which capabilities to even build. You've just switched from regulation (consent-based) to coercion (memo-based). And the next administration might use that same lever.

On Friday a US Commerce Department export-control order blocked foreign nationals from Fable 5 and Mythos 5, and Anthropic shut both models off for every customer rather than try to sort Americans from everyone else. Read quickly, it's a routine export-control story. Washington tightened the gate, the company complied, foreign users lost access.

Europe is reading it differently, and the difference is the whole point. The question Brussels took from Friday wasn't model access. It was who controls the switch.

European governments and companies thought they were buying cloud and AI services. What they were actually holding was permission, granted inside a US legal and infrastructure stack. That distinction stays invisible while everything runs, and becomes the only thing that matters the moment one order can turn the service off overnight, which is exactly what happened. AWS confirmed Anthropic asked it to revoke access for all users in all regions. The server can sit in Frankfurt and the customer in Paris, and the final permission still sits in Washington.

The detail that travels furthest is that even the vendor couldn't keep its own flagship on. Anthropic called the order a misunderstanding, said the jailbreak behind it was narrow and could be pulled from other public models too, and is fighting to restore access. All true, and all beside the point for a European procurement officer. If the company that built the model can be switched off this fast, "buying the service" was never the right verb.

This is why the EU's June 3 sovereignty package suddenly reads less like a policy bundle and more like a sales pitch with good timing. Chips Act 2.0, the Cloud and AI Development Act, an open-source strategy, an energy-AI roadmap. The blunt version is Europe trying to stop renting the most sensitive parts of its stack from someone who can revoke it.

CADA is the load-bearing piece. It sets four sovereignty tiers for cloud and AI, scored on who controls the service and supply chain, where inference data is processed, where the infrastructure sits, and the level of cybersecurity. The top tier wants EU ownership and control, EU-cleared staff, no inference data leaving the bloc, and third-party audits signed off by national authorities. It sounds boring. It's supposed to. Procurement rules are where sovereignty stops being a speech.

The numbers underneath are the harder part. Europe runs more than 80% of its digital stack on non-EU providers, three US hyperscalers hold over 70% of its cloud, and it makes around 10% of the world's chips. Chips Act 2.0 targets €120 billion of investment by 2035, against a 20%-of-global-production goal that most analysts already expect it to miss. CADA wants EU data-center capacity tripled in five to seven years, roughly €200 billion, mostly private. The rules are the easy part. Paying for the infrastructure that makes them usable is the bill.

Korea is sitting in the same seat without the same lever. It runs on the same US AI stack, it has been inside US export-control crossfire before, and its own sovereign-AI talk leans on building the silicon rather than writing the procurement rules. Same lesson Europe just got. Different tool to answer it with.

Sovereign AI used to sound like a slogan. After Friday, it reads like a procurement memo with a large bill stapled to the back. What decides whether it's real is dull on purpose, and it plays out over the next 18 to 24 months in Parliament and Council: the Level 4 cloud rules, the public-sector procurement mandates, the limits on inference data leaving the EU, and who actually funds tripling the data centers. That's the scorecard. The slogan was free. The memo isn't.

Would you buy a supercar just to drive to the corner store for bread? 

That’s exactly what your AI bill looks like when a top-tier model like Fable 5 is being used to do the work of a simple linter. 

Most teams burn through four-figure API bills because of a psychological factor: the fear of getting a bad result. They pick the biggest model at $50 per million output tokens and run refactoring, docstrings, and minor formatting fixes through it. That’s financial suicide.

The key rule of optimization is simple: a model is a gear shifter, not a fixed button.

Instead of relying on a “universal genius,” successful developers redesign their systems around an architecture where a cheap crew is managed by one expensive brain. 

Routine work and boilerplate code generation are handled by Sonnet 4.6 ($15/1M) by default. If a task is genuinely difficult or security-critical, it is automatically escalated to Opus 4.8. Meanwhile, result verification (grading) with simple yes/no decisions is performed by Haiku 4.5, which costs ten times less than the flagship model 

The creator should never grade their own homework, and it certainly makes no sense to pay Fable 5 rates for that job 

This approach completely changes the economics of software development. 

When you separate routine tasks by complexity, enable prompt caching for static context, and send background jobs through the Batch API at half price, your final bill can drop by 71% while maintaining the same code quality [indexes: text].

Start small: move all validation checks and log analysis to Haiku and see what happens to your balance by next week.
